lead: A dental X-ray machine is a small X-ray tube with a pointed cone. It makes one short exposure of a tooth onto film or a digital sensor. The tube has a fixed anode, a tungsten target and oil cooling. A step-up transformer gives the high voltage, and a timer switches it on for a set time. Dentists use it for periapical and bitewing views, and for panoramic imaging. Its design is a lesson in keeping dose low.
prereq: You need: basic X-ray production and the inverse-square law from a first-year physics course.

blocks.text: The tube is a stationary-anode type. A tungsten target sits in a vacuum glass envelope, and insulating oil around it carries heat away. Electrons boiled off the heated filament are accelerated across the tube and hit the target. Most of their energy becomes heat; under 1 % becomes X-rays, mostly braking radiation (bremsstrahlung) with a continuous spectrum, plus the characteristic lines of tungsten. The tube sits in a lead-lined head filled with oil, with one window for the beam. Many dental heads are self-rectified: the tube itself conducts only on the half-cycle when the anode is positive. Newer units use a high-frequency inverter that gives an almost steady tube voltage and a shorter exposure. A step-up transformer raises the mains voltage to the tube voltage, set in kilovolt peak (kVp). The tube current, in milliamperes (mA), sets how many electrons flow. A timer closes the circuit for the exposure time in seconds (s). Dental units typically run at 60 to 70 kVp and 7 to 10 mA for 0.1 to 1 s, giving a few milliampere-seconds (mAs). Exposure quantity is mAs = mA × s. The timer must be accurate because a long exposure raises dose. The exposure button is a dead-man switch on a coiled cord long enough for the operator to stand 2 m away; releasing it stops the exposure at once, and a light and a sound show that X-rays are on.

Inherent filtration comes from the tube wall and oil; added filtration is an aluminium sheet. Total filtration for a dental unit running at 70 kVp or below is at least 1.5 mm aluminium equivalent; units that work above 70 kVp need at least 2.5 mm aluminium. It removes soft X-rays that would only add skin dose. A collimator or lead diaphragm limits the beam to the cone opening. The cone, or position-indicating device, aims the beam at the tooth and sets the target-to-skin distance. A focal spot under 1 mm keeps the image sharp. Film speed or a digital sensor sets the dose needed for a good image.

blocks.where: I₁ and I₂ are beam intensities at distances d₁ and d₂ from the target; dose follows the same ratio.

blocks.text: The cone also sets the beam size. The beam may be no wider than 6 cm at the skin, and rectangular collimation to the size of the sensor cuts the dose further. The focus-to-skin distance must be at least 20 cm for units above 60 kVp; a longer cone also makes the rays more nearly parallel, so the image is less magnified.

An intra-oral periapical film shows the whole tooth and root apex. A bitewing shows crowns and crestal bone of upper and lower teeth in one bite. A panoramic unit (orthopantomogram, OPG) rotates a narrow beam and detector around the head to make one wide image of the jaws; it is not an intra-oral exposure. The operator stands at least 2 m away, behind a lead screen if possible, and wears a lead apron if staying in the room. A lead apron and thyroid collar protect the patient.

sections.h3: Image receptors and keeping the dose low

blocks.text: Film is the oldest receptor; faster film (speed group E or F) needs less exposure. Digital receptors replace it: a wired CCD or CMOS sensor in a thin plastic case gives the image on screen in seconds, and a phosphor storage plate is read by a laser scanner afterwards. Both need less exposure than film, and the image can be enhanced, so retakes fall.

items: Use the fastest receptor and the lowest exposure that gives a diagnostic image.
Collimate to the sensor size and keep the long cone.
Hold the sensor with a holder, never with the patient's or operator's finger.
Cover the patient with a lead apron and thyroid collar.
Avoid retakes by correct aiming and keeping the patient still.
Stand at least 2 m away, out of the beam, and wear a dose badge.

examples.question: A dental unit is set to 70 kVp, 7 mA and 0.6 s. (a) Find the exposure in mAs. (b) The cone is changed from 20 cm to 40 cm target-to-skin distance. By what factor does the skin dose change?
steps: Exposure: mAs = mA × s = 7 mA × 0.6 s = 4.2 mAs.
New skin dose = old dose / 4 = 0.25 of the old dose.
examples.answer: The exposure is 4.2 mAs, and the skin dose falls by a factor of 4 to one quarter of its old value.
examples.check:
mA = 7.0
t = 0.6
d1 = 20.0
d2 = 40.0
mas = mA * t
factor = (d2 / d1) ** 2
fraction = 1 / factor
print(mas)
print(factor)
print(fraction)

examples.question: The dental unit of the first example runs at 70 kVp and 7 mA for 0.6 s with a tungsten target (Z = 74). (a) Find the highest photon energy and the shortest wavelength in the beam. (b) Taking the input power as kVp × mA, find the electrical energy of one exposure. (c) With an X-ray efficiency of about 1.1 × 10⁻⁹ × Z × V, find how much of that energy leaves as X-rays and how much becomes heat.
steps: An electron accelerated through 70 kV gains 70 keV, so no photon can carry more: E<sub>max</sub> = 70 keV.
Shortest wavelength λ<sub>min</sub> = hc ÷ E = 1.24 nm·keV ÷ 70 keV = 0.0177 nm (17.7 pm).
Electrical energy = 70 000 V × 0.007 A × 0.6 s = 294 J (an upper estimate, because the voltage is a peak value).
X-ray energy = 0.0057 × 294 J = 1.7 J; heat in the target = 294 − 1.7 = 292 J.
So 99.4 % of the energy heats the anode, which is why even a short exposure needs a copper-backed target in oil, and why the timer limits the number of exposures per minute.
examples.answer: E<sub>max</sub> = 70 keV and λ<sub>min</sub> = 0.0177 nm; about 294 J goes in, of which only 1.7 J (0.57 %) leaves as X-rays and 292 J becomes heat.

traps: kVp sets penetration and contrast; mA sets quantity. Do not use one for the other.
mAs = mA × s; mA alone is not exposure.
Doubling cone distance cuts dose by 4, not 2 (inverse square).
Timer is in seconds; 0.6 s is not 0.6 ms.

quiz.q: What kVp and mA range is typical for a dental unit?
quiz.a: About 60 to 70 kVp and 7 to 10 mA.

quiz.q: Why is the target made of tungsten?
quiz.a: Tungsten has a high atomic number and a high melting point, so it makes X-rays efficiently and survives heat.

quiz.q: A unit runs at 70 kVp, 7 mA and 0.6 s. Find the exposure in mAs.
The cone length goes from 20 cm to 30 cm. Find the factor by which skin dose changes.
quiz.a: (30/20)² = 2.25, so the new dose is 1/2.25 = 0.44 of the old dose.

quiz.q: What does added aluminium filtration do?
quiz.a: It removes low-energy X-rays that would only add skin dose.

quiz.q: Why does a digital sensor lower patient dose?
quiz.a: It needs fewer X-rays for the same image, so the required mAs and dose can be reduced.

quiz.q: Why must the exposure switch be a dead-man switch on a long cord?
quiz.a: The exposure stops as soon as the button is released, so a stuck or forgotten exposure cannot continue, and the long cord lets the operator stand at least 2 m away, out of the beam, while pressing it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) builds a 3D volume from many projections and is common in implant planning. Rectangular collimation and faster digital sensors cut dose further. Clinics audit dose and check timer accuracy as quality assurance. Search next: dental CBCT, aluminium equivalent filtration, position-indicating device.
